title: Safety reporting, quotas, work-speed data, and retaliation counterpower

observations.claim: OSHA treats injury and illness reporting as protected and identifies points that can lead to future consequences as a possible adverse action.
OSHA recommends worker and union-representative participation, access to safety information and removal of barriers to reporting.
limits: Recommended practice is not a complete adjudication rule.

observations.claim: California AB 701 requires quota disclosure, allows access to recent personal work-speed data and protects complaints about quota effects on breaks and safety.
New York requires quota and work-speed transparency and an injury-reduction program, while preserving anti-retaliation protection.
New York requires worker consultation during injury-reduction program development and worksite evaluation even where no safety committee exists.
limits: Consultation does not equal a general veto over all systems.

observations.claim: Minnesota requires warehouse quota descriptions to include measurement and adverse consequences, and its public materials preserve work-speed and safety-committee controls.

findings.claim: A safety pause can appear to a throughput system as delay, inactivity or underperformance unless the institution preserves a safety exception before scoring.
limits: Does not prove any named metric punished a safety action.

findings.claim: Quota disclosure and worker access to personal work-speed data make the metric and adverse consequence separately contestable.
Worker participation and safety committees create counterpower before injury or discipline by giving affected workers an institutional channel to inspect and change work design.
limits: The strength and composition of the channel vary.

findings.claim: The adverse-action protocol should prohibit use of unexplained inactivity or speed deviations until break, injury, hazard, accommodation and equipment contexts are attached.
